analysis.title: Americas Consumer Finance: Revisting rate caps and late fees post midterms
key_insights: After the midterms, investors are asking whether a Democrat-led Congress could revisit late fee litigation or try new credit card interest rate caps. GS takes no view on the likelihood of any change.
Card issuer loan yields are 27% on a core basis (adjusted for 0% balances). An interest rate cap would pressure issuer profitability and could sharply restrict credit to the real economy.

GS models three cap scenarios: 10% (similar to the January presidential tweet), 18% (the cap on certain credit unions) and 36% (the usury cap for service members). The 10% and 18% scenarios would significantly hit earnings and likely cut credit supply.
A 36% cap is estimated at a more modest 2-3% EPS impact. BFH and SYF would see the largest impact, COF a smaller one and AXP none. Disclosure on balances above 36% is limited, so this is an estimate.

For late fees, GS assumes reductions of 20/35/50% with minimal mitigants. The average 2027E EPS impact across the 4 main card issuers is about 9%. BFH is hit about 22%, SYF about 9%, COF about 4% and AXP about 2%.
Card interest rates average over 17% across the 7 largest issuers but include promo balances and transactors. Adjusted for transactor balances they are closer to the low 20s to low 30s.

Without mitigants, a 10% or 18% cap implies a headwind of roughly 27% to 100% of issuer EPS (Exhibit 5). GS reads this as showing that the economics are challenged when rates are more than 10 points below the 27% average yield.

Issuers would likely respond by underwriting toward prime and super-prime customers, adding account fees, cutting marketing and reducing credit availability. A smaller balance sheet would also free capital to return to shareholders.

Past rate cap attempts failed. The 2025 Sanders/Hawley bill for a 10% cap did not pass, mainly over concerns about credit contraction. A cap was also reportedly considered for the CARD Act of 2009 and dropped for the same reason.

The prior CFPB rule cut late fees from $41 to $8 for issuers with more than 1mn open accounts. The N.D. Texas court vacated it because it did not allow penalty fees reasonable and proportional to violations. GS expects any new effort to have narrower scope and a smaller EPS impact.

GS's late fee sensitivity gives about a 5% EPS headwind for a 20% fee cut, about 9% for 35% and about 13% for 50%. It assumes a $38 average fee, partner revenue-share offsets at BFH/SYF, and mitigation of 20% at BFH/SYF and 30% at COF.

Exhibit 1: 3Q26 card yields are 26.8% at BFH, 21.7% at SYF, 17.7% at COF, 17.3% on average, 16.1% at C, 14.5% at JPM, 12.6% at AXP and 11.5% at BAC. The average is about 700bps above the 10% previously proposed cap. JPM and C yields are implied from call report data.

market_movers.rationale: Buy with a $250 12-month target based on 11.5x 2027E earnings. Risks are further credit deterioration and slower loan growth. Late fee EPS exposure is about 4% in the 35% cut scenario.

Buy with a $360 12-month target based on about 18.0x 2027E EPS. Risks are slower billed business growth and worse credit performance. It has the least exposure to late fees (about 2%) and to a 36% cap (none).
Buy with an $82 12-month target based on 8.0x 2027 EPS. Risks are weaker execution on late fee offsets and weaker consumer health. About 9% EPS exposure in the 35% late fee cut scenario.

Neutral with a $114 12-month target based on 8x 2027 P/E. It is the most exposed issuer, with about 22% EPS impact in the 35% late fee cut scenario. Risks are partner renewal and macro-driven credit deterioration.

sector_views.rationale: GS takes no view on the odds of rate caps or late fee changes. It shows a large gross EPS exposure that is partly offset by mitigants, and expects industry pushback. Ratings are Buy on COF, AXP and SYF and Neutral on BFH.

earnings_insights: Late fee scenarios, 2027E EPS headwind as % of consensus 2027E EPS, for a 20% fee cut: BFH -13%, SYF -5%, COF -2%, AXP -1%. These are GS hypothetical scenario estimates, not reported results.
Late fee scenarios, 35% fee cut: BFH -22%, SYF -9%, COF -4%, AXP -2%. These are GS estimates against Visible Alpha consensus 2027E EPS.
Late fee scenarios, 50% fee cut: BFH -31%, SYF -12%, COF -6%, AXP -3%. These are GS estimates against consensus 2027E EPS, in a range of -3% to -33% across issuers per the exhibit title.

10% rate cap scenario (GS estimate): the EPS headwind is shown as 100% of consensus 2027E EPS for BFH and SYF, and similar for COF and AXP in the exhibit. The 18% cap shows 100% for BFH and SYF, -75% for COF and -27% for AXP.
36% cap on balances yielding 40% (GS estimate): the headwind is -5% of consensus 2027E EPS for BFH, -3% for SYF, -2% for COF and -1% for AXP.

3Q26 inputs: interest income of $1,254mn (BFH), $5,591mn (SYF), $11,360mn (COF, domestic card) and $6,387mn (AXP). Average loans are $18,951mn, $102,278mn, $257,311mn and $231,316mn. Reported loan yields are 26.26%, 21.69%, 17.66% and 10.95%.
TTM late fees assessed are $626mn (BFH, estimated), $2,211mn (SYF), $2,768mn (COF) and $1,003mn (AXP). GS assumes a $38 average fee.

tension_points.bull_case: The industry would push back hard, as it did on late fees. Past cap attempts (the 2025 Sanders/Hawley bill, the 2009 CARD Act) failed over credit availability concerns. Issuers could offset part of the hit by shrinking loan books, tightening underwriting toward prime, adding fees and returning more capital.
tension_points.bear_case: A 10% or 18% cap would cut 27% to 100% of EPS before mitigants against a 27% core yield. It would force large credit supply restrictions. A 36% cap would still hit BFH and SYF most, at 2-3% EPS overall.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Passage of legislation with a cap at 18% or below, or any rate cap that is not limited to balances above 36%.

tension_points.bull_case: The prior rule was vacated in court and any new rule would likely be narrower, with industry pushback. Mitigation through APR optimization and credit tightening offsets 20% (BFH/SYF) to 30% (COF) of the hit, and revenue-share agreements pass part of the cost to partners.
tension_points.bear_case: A 50% reduction in late fees would cut EPS by about 13% on average, with BFH about 31% and SYF about 12%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A new CFPB rule or legislation that cuts late fees by 35% or more, which would put BFH EPS down about 22% or more.

theme_stances.key_argument: A 10% or 18% cap would be a meaningful headwind to EPS, while a 36% cap would be a low-single-digit headwind.
theme_stances.evidence: we take no view on the likelihood of any changes

theme_stances.key_argument: Any new late fee rulemaking would likely face significant industry pushback and could look very different from the original $8 cap proposal.
